RetailAgent / The takeaway

When an agent chooses the wrong moment.

RetailAgent audits sequential long-or-flat decisions using within-stock timing after removing average exposure. The paper reports negative timing and studies how it changes with trajectory shuffling and self-authored memory.

Primary audit−45.7 bps

Text timing, 95% CI [−49.4, −41.8].

↘Sequence control−8.7 bps

↘Behavioral mechanismSelf-conditioning

01The idea

A rising stock can hide a poorly timed policy.

The decision

At each interval, a frozen LLM sees an anonymized price history and chooses long or flat before the next return is revealed. The experiment can also show charts, account state, or the agent’s earlier self-authored memories.

The bottleneck

A policy can benefit from a rising stock while being flat during its strongest intervals. Measuring average exposure and alignment with the next return separately reveals when the policy allocated its exposure.

The idea

Subtract the return of constant exposure on the same stock-day. Audit the remaining timing term, shuffle saved actions to disrupt sequence alignment, and inspect how memory changes the policy’s persistence.

1

Observation comes first

Text, chart, and multimodal pathways supply condition-specific history before the next action. Stock identity, date, news, and fundamentals are concealed in the principal numerical protocol.

2

State is generated by the policy

Position, ledger, account summary, and narrative memories depend on earlier decisions. They make the next prompt partly a consequence of the agent’s own behavior.

3

Separate the optional learned channel

The soft-token encoder has a training stage. The standard and narrative conditions use a frozen LLM for inference, with observations and carried state specified by each condition.

How the method works

  1. 01

    Control the information

    Show anonymized intraday history, then require a long-or-flat decision before the next return.

  2. 02

    Remove mean exposure

    Compare each schedule with constant exposure on the same realized stock-day.

  3. 03

    Disrupt the sequence

    Shuffle saved actions and examine matched memory panels to characterize sequential structure.

The comparison stays on the same price path

A stock’s overall movement affects both an agent and a constant-exposure comparator. Subtracting that comparator focuses the score on when the agent allocated its exposure. Negative timing means relatively unfavorable allocation on the evaluated path.

02Explore

Make the idea tangible.

Same exposure, different timing

Toggle whether a toy agent is long or flat before each interval. Returns are fixed at −20, +15, −10, +25, −15, and +5 basis points.

The paper’s timing formula is evaluated on six synthetic returns. Inverting the schedule negates its centered timing score.

In practice

An audit for sequential agents

Exposure-matched timing diagnoses the agent’s interval choices on historical price paths. The study measures cross-sectional stock selection separately through IC and uses saved-action shuffles to examine sequential alignment.

What to notice

The one-earlier-memory condition has the most negative timing of these four. In the later-period panel, it also makes fewer position changes: 1.7 per stock-day versus 2.5 for current memory only. Timing varies non-monotonically with memory-window length.

Experiment setup and comparison details

Each main-period arm attempts 1,500 stock-days across 150 dates. Scored N excludes failed intervals and constant-action trajectories, so the timing estimates condition on both actions appearing. Position-change counts come from the separate later-period panel.

Equation 2

Exposure plus timing

The action-weighted return decomposes exactly into average exposure times the day’s return plus centered timing. Always-long and always-flat policies score zero timing; complementing every action negates the timing score.

Compare within the recorded panel

Modalities, model families, and state conditions are evaluated in their recorded sampling frames. The panel definitions and stock-day counts specify which action traces contribute to each timing estimate.

Read the statement ↗
Reasoning behind the formulation

Center the action sequence

For a stock-day, pˉid\bar p_{id}pˉ​id​ is the fraction of intervals spent long. The constant-exposure comparator earns pˉid\bar p_{id}pˉ​id​ times the sum of interval returns. Subtracting it from the schedule’s return gives the timing sum shown below.

Separate direction from sequential alignment

A policy that is always long or always flat has zero centered timing. A nonzero score requires variation in its actions and alignment with subsequent returns. This explains why action persistence and switching behavior matter to the audit.

Read controls within their sampling frame

Same-day shuffling preserves each day’s action count while breaking interval alignment. Global shuffling draws from the saved archive. Each modality and memory panel specifies its stock-day frame, conditioning, and sample count.

Assumptions behind the analysis

RetailAgent audits directional and sequential policy structure on historical equity paths with controlled decision-time information. Equation 1 defines exposure-matched timing, and the experimental panels specify the observed policies, state conditions, and sampling frames.

Equation 1 · Timing decomposition in the paper

Questions worth asking

What does inverting a schedule reveal?

On a fixed research-return path, complementing every long-or-flat action negates centered timing while preserving the same sequence of returns. This gives a sign diagnostic for the saved action trace.

How is the memory window counted?

The two-pass protocol creates a current-step memory. The window w counts earlier memories, so w=0w=0w=0 provides the current memory and w=1w=1w=1 adds one earlier memory.

Continue the research thread

RetailAgent focuses on the timing of sequential choices. SURF offers another view of decision quality: how well a set of choices represents different objective trade-offs.
